Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 106, verses 1–4:

Meccan, and its verses are 4. "It was revealed after al-Tin."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿For the covenant (ilaf) of the Quraysh﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿let them worship﴾.

He commanded them to worship Him on account of their covenant of the two journeys. If you say: why was the fa' (then) introduced? I say: because of the sense of conditionality in the statement, for the meaning is: "If not, then let them worship Him for their covenant," in the sense that: God's blessings upon them are beyond counting; so if they do not worship Him for all His other blessings, let them worship Him for this single one, which is a manifest blessing. It has also been said that the meaning is: "Be amazed at the covenant of the Quraysh." And it has been said: it is connected to what precedes it, meaning: "So He made them like chewed-up husks, for the covenant of the Quraysh." This is in the position of tadmin (interlocking) in poetry, which is when the meaning of a verse depends on the verse before it in a way that cannot be sound except with it. In the codex of Ubayy, the two are a single surah without separation. It is reported from Umar that he recited both in the second rak'ah of the Maghrib prayer, and in the first he recited "By the fig" [this is how it occurs in al-Tha'labi. 'Amr ibn Maymun said: I prayed behind Umar at Maghrib, and he mentioned the hadith. Likewise 'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Shaybah linked it from the narration of Abu Ishaq from 'Amr ibn Maymun, who said: "Umar led us in the Maghrib prayer. In the first rak'ah he recited 'By the fig,' and in the second, 'Have you not seen' and 'For the covenant of the Quraysh.'"].

The meaning is that He destroyed the Abyssinians who intended them, so that people would hear of this and dread them more, and honour them with greater reverence, until security was secured for them in their two journeys, and no one would dare to attack them. The Quraysh had two journeys: they set out in winter to Yemen and in summer to Syria, trading and seeking provisions, and they were secure in their two journeys because they were the people of the Sacred Precinct of Allah and the custodians of His House, so no one would harm them, while the people other than them were snatched away and raided.

The word ilaf comes from your saying: "I accustomed (alaftu) the place, ualifuhu, ilafan," meaning: when I became familiar with it; so I am mu'allif (one who is accustomed). He said:

[I tightened the saddle upon you above a swift she-camel... among the accustomed ones, the easy-paced, not the wild ones of the thickets]

The shamlah with shaddah; the shamlal and the shamil: the light, swift in its going. That is: I tightened the saddle upon a swift-paced she-camel, heading to you, and that she-camel is one of the accustomed camels, that is, of easy and straight gait. It is also transmitted as al-zahw with a zay, which is its going after reaching water. The awarik is the plural of arikah: those that remain in the place of the arak tree, grazing on it, or grazing on a plant called al-hamd; that is, they are not like those tied up with fodder and made noble for travel.

It is also read: li-ilaf (li'lāf) Quraysh, meaning: for the close companionship of Quraysh. It has been said: one says alifahu, ilfan and ilafan. Abu Ja'far read: li-ilf Quraysh. Someone combined both:

["You claim that your brothers, the Quraysh, have companionship (ilf), while you have no covenant (ilaf)... those men were secure from hunger and fear, while the Banu Asad went hungry and feared." This was said by Musawwar ibn Hind ibn Qays, addressing the Banu Asad. "Quraysh" is the predicate. Their saying "they have companionship" is a resumption to explain their lie. Al-alf and al-alaf are the verbal noun of alifahu, when one loves someone, becomes accustomed to him and does not shun him. Alafa ilafan between them means: he made a bond of companionship between them. The Quraysh combined the winter and summer journeys, one time setting out on this one and another time on that one, without fear or dread.] "Those" refers to the Quraysh. "Amanu" is in the passive voice: that is, their Lord secured them from hunger and fear, when the Banu Asad went hungry and feared. He turned to the third person as an indication of turning away from them and of amazement at others concerning their condition.

Ikrimah read: li-yu'lif Quraysh ilafahum, the journey of winter and summer.

Quraysh are the descendants of al-Nadr ibn Kinanah. They were named with the diminutive of al-qirsh, which is a great creature in the sea that harasses ships and can be subdued only by fire. It is reported from Mu'awiyah that he asked Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "Why were the Quraysh named so?" He said: "After a creature in the sea that eats and is not eaten, and rises and is not overcome." And he recited:

[The Quraysh are those who dwell in the sea; by them the Quraysh were named Quraysh. It devours the lean and the fat and leaves nothing... one feather of any winged thing... Thus it is in the Book the Quraysh attained; they eat the lands, eating greedily... And among them is a final-time prophet who multiplies slaughter and wounds among them... He fills the earth with cavalry and infantry, gathering the rain in a fierce gathering.]

For the Tubba'. The Quraysh is the diminutive of qarsh. Ibn Abbas said: a creature in the sea that eats and is not eaten, so it was diminutive and the name was given to al-Nadr ibn Kinanah, then his children were named by it. The narrators hold that it is the name of Fihr ibn Malik ibn al-Nadr. The Rafidah said it is the name of Qusayy ibn Kilab, and by this they reached the negation of the imamate of Abu Bakr and Umar, because they were not Qurashi, since they join with him (ﷺ) after Qusayy, and the imamate is from Quraysh. Quraysh is the subject, and the sentence after it is a resumed clause explaining it; and "by them it was named" is the predicate, meaning: by reason of it this tribe was named Quraysh, which eats; that is, the Quraysh of the sea. This is supported by what is transmitted before this verse, which is:

[You were raised with height in the depth of the sea, over all the seas, armies... it eats.]

It may also be that it is the dabilah (a kind of creature).

Al-ghath is the wicked; al-samin is the good. The owner of the two wings is a metaphor for birds, or a metaphor for the wealthy, and he exaggerated that it does not leave or spare anything it seizes, by saying that it does not leave the feathers of the winged one. It is transmitted as "fihi" instead of "yawman," and this refers to the Quraysh of the sea. "Thus" is a reference to the state of the sea creature, or to what he himself said. "The Book" means the Torah or the Gospel, or the books of history. Quraysh here is the tribe. It is transmitted:

[Thus in the lands is the tribe of Quraysh, eating the lands... ]

That is: they take their wealth. Al-kushaysh originally means a hidden sound, that is, eating with ease, without terror or weariness; it is then a metaphor. "The Prophet" is Muhammad (ﷺ). Khamasha: he scratched him. Al-khumush: scratches. Al-khaylah: a distant figure. Al-khayl: horsemen. Al-rijal: those on foot. "They gather" is an attribute of rijal, and it is distant that it refers back to Quraysh. Al-kumaysh: swift. Al-muntadam: the cutting; that is, they gather it quickly, but the meaning of al-khumush here is wounds.

The diminutive is for magnification. It has been said: it derives from al-qarsh, which is earning, because they were earners through their trade and their travelling in the lands. They were given the ilaf unrestricted and then it was replaced with the restriction to the two journeys, to magnify the matter of the covenant and to remind of the great blessing in it. The journey is put in the accusative as an object by their ilaf, just as yatiman is put in the accusative by ith'am. He meant the journeys of winter and summer, and he used the singular for avoidance of confusion, as in the poet's line:

["Eat in part of your bellies..."]

Read "rihlah" with a damma: it is the direction to which one travels. The indefinite in "jū'in" and "khawf" is for their intensity: that is, He fed them through the two journeys from severe hunger they had been in before them, and secured them from a great fear, which was the fear of the people of the Elephant, or the fear of being snatched in their land and on their routes. It has been said: they had been struck by hardship until they ate carrion and burnt bones, and He secured them from the fear of leprosy so that it would not strike them in their land. It has been said all of that was by the supplication of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. Among the innovated interpretations: "and secured them from fear," that the caliphate might be in others. It is also read "min khawf" with the nun concealed.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites the surah of Li-ilaf Quraysh, Allah gives him ten good deeds for the number of those who circumambulated the Ka'bah and performed i'tikaf in it." [Reported by al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi and Ibn Mardawayh with a chain to Ubayy ibn Ka'b.]

Likewise 'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Shaybah linked it from the narration of Abu Ishaq from 'Amr ibn Maymun, who said: "Umar led us in the Maghrib prayer. In the first rak'ah he recited 'By the fig,' and in the second, 'Have you not seen' and 'For the covenant of the Quraysh.'"].

The meaning is that He destroyed the Abyssinians who intended them, so that people would hear of this and dread them more, and honour them with greater reverence, until security was secured for them in their two journeys, and no one would dare to attack them. The Quraysh had two journeys: they set out in winter to Yemen and in summer to Syria, trading and seeking provisions, and they were secure in their two journeys because they were the people of the Sacred Precinct of Allah and the custodians of His House, so no one would harm them, while the people other than them were snatched away and raided.

The word ilaf comes from your saying: "I accustomed (alaftu) the place, ualifuhu, ilafan," meaning: when I became familiar with it; so I am mu'allif (one who is accustomed). He said:

[I tightened the saddle upon you above a swift she-camel... among the accustomed ones, the easy-paced, not the wild ones of the thickets]

The shamlah with shaddah; the shamlal and the shamil: the light, swift in its going. That is: I tightened the saddle upon a swift-paced she-camel, heading to you, and that she-camel is one of the accustomed camels, that is, of easy and straight gait. It is also transmitted as al-zahw with a zay, which is its going after reaching water. The awarik is the plural of arikah: those that remain in the place of the arak tree, grazing on it, or grazing on a plant called al-hamd; that is, they are not like those tied up with fodder and made noble for travel.

It is also read: li-ilaf (li'lāf) Quraysh, meaning: for the close companionship of Quraysh. It has been said: one says alifahu, ilfan and ilafan. Abu Ja'far read: li-ilf Quraysh. Someone combined both:

["You claim that your brothers, the Quraysh, have companionship (ilf), while you have no covenant (ilaf)... those men were secure from hunger and fear, while the Banu Asad went hungry and feared." This was said by Musawwar ibn Hind ibn Qays, addressing the Banu Asad. "Quraysh" is the predicate. Their saying "they have companionship" is a resumption to explain their lie. Al-alf and al-alaf are the verbal noun of alifahu, when one loves someone, becomes accustomed to him and does not shun him. Alafa ilafan between them means: he made a bond of companionship between them. The Quraysh combined the winter and summer journeys, one time setting out on this one and another time on that one, without fear or dread.] "Those" refers to the Quraysh. "Amanu" is in the passive voice: that is, their Lord secured them from hunger and fear, when the Banu Asad went hungry and feared. He turned to the third person as an indication of turning away from them and of amazement at others concerning their condition.

Ikrimah read: li-yu'lif Quraysh ilafahum, the journey of winter and summer.

Quraysh are the descendants of al-Nadr ibn Kinanah. They were named with the diminutive of al-qirsh, which is a great creature in the sea that harasses ships and can be subdued only by fire. It is reported from Mu'awiyah that he asked Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "Why were the Quraysh named so?" He said: "After a creature in the sea that eats and is not eaten, and rises and is not overcome." And he recited:

[The Quraysh are those who dwell in the sea; by them the Quraysh were named Quraysh. It devours the lean and the fat and leaves nothing... one feather of any winged thing... Thus it is in the Book the Quraysh attained; they eat the lands, eating greedily... And among them is a final-time prophet who multiplies slaughter and wounds among them... He fills the earth with cavalry and infantry, gathering the rain in a fierce gathering.]

For the Tubba'. The Quraysh is the diminutive of qarsh. Ibn Abbas said: a creature in the sea that eats and is not eaten, so it was diminutive and the name was given to al-Nadr ibn Kinanah, then his children were named by it. The narrators hold that it is the name of Fihr ibn Malik ibn al-Nadr. The Rafidah said it is the name of Qusayy ibn Kilab, and by this they reached the negation of the imamate of Abu Bakr and Umar, because they were not Qurashi, since they join with him (ﷺ) after Qusayy, and the imamate is from Quraysh. Quraysh is the subject, and the sentence after it is a resumed clause explaining it; and "by them it was named" is the predicate, meaning: by reason of it this tribe was named Quraysh, which eats; that is, the Quraysh of the sea. This is supported by what is transmitted before this verse, which is:

[You were raised with height in the depth of the sea, over all the seas, armies... it eats.]

It may also be that it is the dabilah (a kind of creature).

Al-ghath is the wicked; al-samin is the good. The owner of the two wings is a metaphor for birds, or a metaphor for the wealthy, and he exaggerated that it does not leave or spare anything it seizes, by saying that it does not leave the feathers of the winged one. It is transmitted as "fihi" instead of "yawman," and this refers to the Quraysh of the sea. "Thus" is a reference to the state of the sea creature, or to what he himself said. "The Book" means the Torah or the Gospel, or the books of history. Quraysh here is the tribe. It is transmitted:

[Thus in the lands is the tribe of Quraysh, eating the lands... ]

That is: they take their wealth. Al-kushaysh originally means a hidden sound, that is, eating with ease, without terror or weariness; it is then a metaphor. "The Prophet" is Muhammad (ﷺ). Khamasha: he scratched him. Al-khumush: scratches. Al-khaylah: a distant figure. Al-khayl: horsemen. Al-rijal: those on foot. "They gather" is an attribute of rijal, and it is distant that it refers back to Quraysh. Al-kumaysh: swift. Al-muntadam: the cutting; that is, they gather it quickly, but the meaning of al-khumush here is wounds.

The diminutive is for magnification. It has been said: it derives from al-qarsh, which is earning, because they were earners through their trade and their travelling in the lands. They were given the ilaf unrestricted and then it was replaced with the restriction to the two journeys, to magnify the matter of the covenant and to remind of the great blessing in it. The journey is put in the accusative as an object by their ilaf, just as yatiman is put in the accusative by ith'am. He meant the journeys of winter and summer, and he used the singular for avoidance of confusion, as in the poet's line:

["Eat in part of your bellies..."]

Read "rihlah" with a damma: it is the direction to which one travels. The indefinite in "jū'in" and "khawf" is for their intensity: that is, He fed them through the two journeys from severe hunger they had been in before them, and secured them from a great fear, which was the fear of the people of the Elephant, or the fear of being snatched in their land and on their routes. It has been said: they had been struck by hardship until they ate carrion and burnt bones, and He secured them from the fear of leprosy so that it would not strike them in their land. It has been said all of that was by the supplication of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. Among the innovated interpretations: "and secured them from fear," that the caliphate might be in others. It is also read "min khawf" with the nun concealed.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites the surah of Li-ilaf Quraysh, Allah gives him ten good deeds for the number of those who circumambulated the Ka'bah and performed i'tikaf in it." [Reported by al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi and Ibn Mardawayh with a chain to Ubayy ibn Ka'b.]
